Chapter 2: Understanding the Stories That Shape Us.
Think about it for a second—every one of us carries around a set of stories. Some are handed down by others, some we create ourselves just to make sense of the world. These stories? They quietly shape how we live, what we expect, and what we think is even possible. Most of the time, they’re just running in the background, gently nudging our choices and reactions without us even noticing.
Picture this: A young professional grows up hearing, “hard work always pays off.” She throws herself into her job—stays late, volunteers for every extra project. But when those promotions don’t come, she feels let down. Not just by her company, but by the story she believed in. After months of feeling frustrated, she finally realizes—her value isn’t tied to how much she works. And sometimes, let’s be honest, the system just isn’t fair. That story she trusted? It was only part of the truth.
Or think about someone raised in a family where stability was everything. Every time a chance for adventure popped up, he hesitated. He’d watch his friends travel or launch new businesses, but he’d always find a reason to stay put. The story in his head kept whispering: “Risk is dangerous. Comfort’s what matters most.” It wasn’t until he met someone who’d lost everything and rebuilt their life that he started to wonder—maybe playing it safe isn’t the same as being happy.
And these stories? They’re not just about jobs or money. They reach into every corner of life—our relationships, our health, even how we see ourselves. Take a woman who’s struggled with her weight for years. She remembers being called “the chubby one” as a kid, and that label stuck. It shaped how she saw herself for decades. But when she finally started looking at herself through her own eyes—not through the words of others—she began making changes that felt good, not like punishment.
Most of us don’t even realize how much these old stories are steering our lives. They get so familiar, they start to feel like unshakable facts. But if we pause and reflect, patterns start to pop up. Suddenly, it’s clear—so many of our limits are self-imposed, built on stories that might be outdated or just plain incomplete.
That’s where self-reflection comes in. And no, it’s not about blaming your parents, your teachers, or society. It’s about getting curious. Asking, “Where did this belief come from? Is it actually helping me? And what could happen if I just let it go?”
There’s a man who always felt like an outsider. He traced that feeling back to one single moment as a kid, when he was left out of a game. That memory grew into a story: “I don’t belong.” But when he saw it for what it was—just one event, not his whole life—he started to take small risks. He joined groups, reached out, and little by little, that old story lost its grip.
Changing these stories isn’t easy. Our brains love what’s familiar, even if it hurts. But with practice, new stories can be written. Someone who once believed they were unlucky in love can begin to see themselves as a person learning to connect. Someone who always thought they were “bad with money” can grow into a careful, confident steward of their resources.
It all starts with awareness. When you start to notice the stories that play on repeat, you get to choose which ones to keep—and which ones to rewrite. Over time, these new narratives shape new actions, and those actions? They create brand new outcomes.
